ox: Incorrect. This is the NORMAL cell direction (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in), but in an inside-out vesicle the pump faces the opposite way, so relative to the vesicle the directions are reversed.
Incorrect. The pump is an antiporter: it moves Na⁺ and K⁺ in OPPOSITE directions, never both the same way.
Incorrect. In an inside-out vesicle the cytoplasmic face of the pump points toward the surrounding medium, so ATP added outside reaches its binding site. The pump works.

Correct. The pump always moves Na⁺ away from its ATP-binding (cytoplasmic) face and K⁺ toward it. In an inside-out vesicle that face is the outside medium, so Na⁺ goes INTO the vesicle and K⁺ goes OUT into the medium.

p: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses one ATP per cycle on its cytoplasmic face, moving 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in. Its directions are fixed relative to its own faces, not to which side is 'outside'. In an inside-out vesicle the cytoplasmic face points into the surrounding medium, so every direction flips relative to the vesicle.

x2A_054.trap: Applying the normal-cell direction without checking which face of the pump can reach the ATP.
x2A_054.eli: A water pump only works if you push its handle from one side. Flip the pump around and it moves water the opposite way relative to the bucket.
mem: Per ATP: 3 Na⁺ OUT of the cell, 2 K⁺ IN.
ATP binds on the cytoplasmic (inner) face.
Inside-out vesicle: cytoplasmic face points to the medium, so directions reverse.
x2A_054.sc: Find the face where ATP is. Na⁺ always leaves that face; K⁺ always arrives at it.
x2A_054.mn: 3 Na out, 2 K in: 'Na leaves the ATP side, K keeps coming to it.'

ox: Correct. The protein is made on the rough ER, sent to the Golgi for processing, packed into secretory vesicles, and released by exocytosis at the plasma membrane.
Wrong. This puts the Golgi before the rough ER. Also, lysosomes digest material and are not on the secretion route.
Wrong. The nucleus holds DNA but does not make secreted proteins. The route also ends in a lysosome, not at the cell surface.
Wrong. Smooth ER makes lipids, not secreted proteins. Peroxisomes handle oxidative reactions and are not on this route.

p: Proteins to be exported are built by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum (ER), which is studded with ribosomes. They enter the ER space as they are made.
Vesicles (small membrane bubbles) carry them to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them. Secretory vesicles then fuse with the plasma membrane and release them outside (exocytosis).

d_2A_10.eli: It is like a factory line: build the product, wrap and label it, load it on a truck, and deliver it out the front door.
mem: Order: rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, plasma membrane.
Rough ER makes secreted and membrane proteins.
Lysosome is a different destination from secretion.
d_2A_10.trap: Reversing the order of the ER and Golgi, or sending the protein to a lysosome.

ox: Wrong. Stratified squamous has many layers and protects, like skin. Gas would diffuse too slowly through it.
Wrong. This lines the larger airways and uses cilia to sweep mucus. It is too thick for gas exchange.
Correct. One thin layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance, so gases pass quickly between air and blood.
Wrong. Columnar cells are tall, built for absorption and secretion. The extra thickness slows diffusion.

p: Epithelium is tissue that covers surfaces. Simple means one layer; stratified means many layers. Squamous means flat; columnar means tall.
Gas moves by diffusion, which is faster over a short distance. A single layer of flat cells is the thinnest option, so it fits the alveoli and capillary walls.

d_2A_17.eli: Passing a note through a thin sheet of paper is easy. Passing it through a thick book is not.
mem: Simple squamous: diffusion (alveoli, capillaries).
Stratified squamous: protection (skin).
Simple columnar: absorption (gut); ciliated pseudostratified: airways.
d_2A_17.trap: Choosing the tougher, protective epithelium. Exchange needs thin, not tough.
d_2A_17.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. SGLT pulls glucose in using the Na+ gradient made by the Na+/K+ ATPase. Without the pump, the gradient fades and glucose uptake falls.
Wrong. Blocking the pump does not give more useful Na+. The Na+ gradient collapses, and the gradient is what drives SGLT.
Wrong. SGLT does not use ATP directly. It is secondary active transport, using the Na+ gradient that ATP built.
Wrong. Glucose does not flow in reverse. The transporter simply loses its driving force and slows down.

p: Primary active transport uses ATP directly. The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps Na+ out of the cell, creating a low-Na+ inside.
Secondary active transport uses that stored gradient. SGLT lets Na+ flow in, and glucose comes along. If the pump is blocked, the gradient is lost and so is the glucose uptake.

d_2A_3.eli: A water slide only works if someone keeps carrying water up the hill. Stop the carrying and the slide stops.
mem: Na+/K+ ATPase = primary active transport; it sets the gradient.
SGLT = secondary active, symport of Na+ and glucose.
Ouabain and digoxin inhibit the Na+/K+ ATPase.
d_2A_3.trap: Believing a cotransporter uses ATP itself. It uses the gradient made by an ATP pump.
d_2A_3.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Each cycle uses 1 ATP, pumps 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. This makes the pump electrogenic (it adds a net positive charge outside).
Wrong. This reverses the numbers. Remember that 3 goes with Na+ and 2 goes with K+.
Wrong. This has the right numbers but wrong directions. Na+ goes out and K+ goes in.
Wrong. The pump is not 1:1. The 3:2 ratio is what makes it electrogenic.

p: This pump sits in the plasma membrane and uses ATP to move ions against their gradients. It keeps Na+ low and K+ high inside the cell.
Each cycle removes 3 positive charges (Na+) and brings in only 2 (K+). The cell inside gets slightly more negative.

q20.eli: Think of a door where 3 people leave and only 2 enter each time. The room slowly empties.
mem: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, 1 ATP per cycle.
Electrogenic: helps make the inside negative.
Na+ outside is high; K+ inside is high.
q20.trap: Swapping the numbers or directions. Say it as 'Na out 3, K in 2.'
q20.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Smooth ER has no ribosomes. It makes lipids, detoxifies drugs, and stores calcium.
Correct. Ribosomes on the rough ER push the new protein into the ER lumen, the start of the route to secretion or the membrane.
Wrong. Mitochondria make ATP and a few of their own proteins, not secreted proteins.
Wrong. Lysosomes digest waste and old parts. They do not build secretory proteins.

p: The rough ER has ribosomes (protein-building machines) attached to its surface, giving it a bumpy look. The proteins are fed into the ER's inner space as they are made.
From there they travel to the Golgi and then to the cell surface, outside, or lysosomes.

q21.eli: The rough ER is a bakery kitchen with workers (ribosomes) at the counters, making goods meant for delivery.
mem: Rough ER: protein synthesis for secretion and membranes.
Smooth ER: lipids, detox, Ca2+ storage.
Free ribosomes make proteins used inside the cytosol.
q21.trap: Choosing the smooth ER because it sounds like the main ER. Look for ribosomes.
q21.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Gap junctions are channels that let ions and small molecules pass between cells, so they connect cells rather than seal them.
Correct. Tight junctions seal the space between neighboring cells so fluid cannot leak through. This forces material to pass through the cells.
Wrong. Desmosomes are like spot welds that hold cells together against stretching but do not seal.
Wrong. Hemidesmosomes hold the cell to the basement membrane below, not to its neighbors, and do not seal.

p: Epithelial cells line surfaces such as the gut and skin. Junctions are the connections between them. Different junctions do different jobs: seal, anchor, or communicate.
Tight junctions form a belt around each cell so the space between cells is blocked. This makes the epithelium a barrier.

q22.eli: Tight junction is like caulk sealing a bathtub. Desmosomes are like screws. Gap junctions are like small doors.
mem: Tight = seal. Desmosome = anchor. Gap = communicate.
Hemidesmosome anchors to the basement membrane.
Tight junctions give polarity and barrier function.
q22.trap: Confusing anchoring junctions (desmosomes) with sealing junctions.
q22.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. This is the older Davson-Danielli model, with protein sheets on both sides of lipid. Later evidence showed proteins are embedded in the bilayer.
Wrong. Flip-flop of phospholipids between leaflets is slow because the polar head must pass through the oily core. It needs flippase enzymes. Lateral movement is the fast kind.
Wrong. The bilayer is fluid, not a rigid lattice. Many proteins drift sideways, as experiments such as FRAP show.
Correct. The membrane is a 2D fluid. Lipids and many proteins slide sideways in their own leaflet, and proteins are scattered like a mosaic.

p: A plasma membrane is a bilayer: two layers of phospholipids with water-loving heads outside and oily tails inside. Proteins are embedded in it or attached to it.
Fluid means the parts can move sideways. Mosaic means proteins are scattered in a pattern, like tiles. Moving from one layer to the other is rare and slow.

x2A_001.eli: Think of a crowded dance floor where people slide around freely, but no one can easily jump to the floor above.
mem: Lateral diffusion is fast; flip-flop is slow without flippase.
Proteins can be integral (embedded) or peripheral (attached).
Fluid mosaic replaced the protein-sandwich model.
x2A_001.trap: Believing lipids flip easily between leaflets, or that proteins are fixed in place.
x2A_001.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. This is the effect of cholesterol at high temperature, where it restrains tail motion. In the cold, it does the opposite.
Wrong. Cholesterol lowers permeability to ions and small polar molecules because it fills gaps between lipids.
Wrong. Cholesterol is not an enzyme. Flippases catalyze lipid flip-flop.
Correct. Cholesterol's rigid ring wedges between the fatty acid tails so they cannot pack tightly into a gel, which keeps the membrane fluid in the cold.

p: Membrane fluidity changes with temperature. In the cold, lipid tails pack tightly and the membrane stiffens. When warm, the tails move more and the membrane becomes loose.
Cholesterol sits between the tails. In the cold it blocks tight packing, raising fluidity. In the heat it limits tail motion, lowering fluidity.

x2A_002.eli: Cholesterol is like putting a few pencils between stacked papers. In the cold it stops them from stacking flat. When things get wild, it keeps them from sliding all over.
mem: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer.
Cold: prevents packing, so more fluid. Hot: restrains motion, so less fluid.
Unsaturated tails also raise fluidity; longer, saturated tails lower it.
x2A_002.trap: Saying cholesterol always makes membranes more rigid. It depends on temperature.
x2A_002.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. A phospholipid head is polar or charged and loves water. To flip, it must travel through the oily, nonpolar middle of the bilayer. That costs a lot of energy, so flipping is very slow without help.
Wrong. Most phospholipids are not covalently attached to proteins. The trap is thinking that 'stuck' means chemically bonded.
Wrong. Lateral diffusion (sliding sideways in the same leaflet) is fast, because the head stays in water. The trap is lumping all lipid motion together.
Wrong. The cytoskeleton holds some proteins in place, not each lipid. The trap is overgeneralizing from proteins to lipids.

p: A membrane is a double layer of lipids. Each lipid has a water-loving (polar) head and oily (nonpolar) tails. The tails face inward and form an oily core. A leaflet is one of the two layers.
Flip-flop means a lipid moves from one leaflet to the other. Its polar head must cross the oily core. That is a big energy barrier. Enzymes called flippases can speed it up.

x2A_004.eli: Imagine a kid who loves swimming being forced to cross a field of thick mud to reach the other pool. They will not do it often.
mem: Flip-flop is slow (hours to days) without flippases.
Lateral diffusion within a leaflet is fast.
The barrier is the polar head crossing the nonpolar core.
x2A_004.trap: Do not confuse slow flip-flop with slow sideways movement. Sideways movement is fast.
x2A_004.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Simple diffusion rises in a straight line with concentration and never levels off. The trap is ignoring the saturation clue.
Wrong. Primary active transport needs ATP and can pile up X inside. Here ATP block changes nothing and X never builds up.
Wrong. Secondary active transport can move X uphill using an ion gradient, and that gradient depends on ATP. Here nothing is uphill and ATP does not matter.
Correct. Leveling off means a limited number of carrier proteins are all busy. No ATP needed and no uphill movement means it moves only down its gradient. That is facilitated diffusion.

p: Some molecules cannot cross the oily membrane alone. A carrier protein helps them move down their concentration gradient (high to low). No energy is spent.
Carriers can get full. When every carrier is busy, uptake stops rising. This is called saturation. Simple diffusion never saturates.

x2A_007.eli: A revolving door with only a few slots. Past a certain crowd size, more people outside cannot go through any faster.
mem: Saturable plus no energy plus downhill = facilitated diffusion.
Simple diffusion is linear and not saturable.
Active transport can go uphill and needs energy (direct or indirect).
x2A_007.trap: Saturation alone rules out simple diffusion, but you also need the no-ATP and no-uphill clues to rule out active transport.
x2A_007.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The solution is isosmotic (same total solute count), but that is not the same as isotonic. Urea crosses freely, so it does not count for tonicity. The trap is equating osmolarity with tonicity.
Wrong. Shrinking needs a solute that cannot enter, at higher concentration outside. Urea can enter.
Correct. Urea flows into the cell until inside and outside match. Then the cell's own trapped solutes still pull water in. The cell swells and bursts (lyses). The solution is isosmotic but hypotonic.
Wrong. Urea does not stay outside to hold water out. The cell does not stay shrunken. Any brief change is reversed as urea enters.

p: Osmolarity counts all dissolved particles. Tonicity counts only particles that cannot cross the membrane. Only those hold water in place.
Urea crosses a red cell membrane easily. So it adds no lasting pull on water. The solutes trapped inside the cell then draw water in, and the cell swells.

x2A_008.eli: If the door between two rooms is open, people mix freely and nobody is stuck on one side. Only people who cannot pass the door make one room more crowded.
mem: Tonicity depends only on non-penetrating solutes.
Isosmotic does not mean isotonic.
Permeable solute plus red cell in it = swell and lyse (hypotonic effect).
x2A_008.trap: Seeing 300 mOsm = 300 mOsm and picking 'nothing happens'. Always ask whether the solute can cross.
x2A_008.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Na+ is much more concentrated outside the cell. Na+ rushing in releases energy. The symporter uses that energy to pull glucose in against its gradient. This is secondary active transport.
Wrong. The symporter does not break down ATP itself. The trap is thinking that all active transport uses ATP directly (that is primary).
Wrong. The question says glucose is moving against its gradient, so its gradient cannot be the energy source.
Wrong. That gradient belongs to the mitochondria and drives ATP synthase. It is not used at the plasma membrane.

p: A cell keeps Na+ low inside using the Na+/K+ pump, which uses ATP. That creates a stored energy, like water behind a dam.
A symporter moves two things the same direction. Na+ goes downhill and carries glucose uphill. ATP is used only indirectly, to keep the Na+ gradient.

x2A_013.eli: A waterwheel: water falling downhill turns the wheel, which lifts a bucket of something else uphill.
mem: SGLT = Na+-glucose symporter = secondary active transport.
Energy comes from the Na+ gradient, kept by Na+/K+-ATPase.
Primary active transport uses ATP directly.
x2A_013.trap: Choosing ATP because ATP is involved somewhere. The question asks for the immediate energy source.
x2A_013.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The substances move in opposite directions, so it is not a symporter. It also uses no ATP directly, so it is not primary.
Wrong. A uniporter moves only one substance. Here two substances move, and the transmitter is pushed uphill.
Correct. Transmitter goes in while H+ goes out, which is opposite directions: antiporter. The energy comes from the H+ gradient, so it is secondary active transport.
Wrong. A pump hydrolyzes ATP itself. This protein uses the gradient made by a different pump (the V-type ATPase).

p: Ask two questions. First, how many substances move and in which direction? One substance is a uniporter. Two the same way is a symporter. Two opposite ways is an antiporter.
Second, where does the energy come from? ATP hydrolysis by the protein itself is primary. A gradient made by another pump is secondary.

x2A_014.eli: A seesaw: one kid goes up as another goes down, and someone else pushed the seesaw's energy in first.
mem: Opposite directions = antiporter; same direction = symporter.
Uses an existing gradient = secondary active.
Uses ATP directly = primary active (a pump).
x2A_014.trap: Mixing up the direction label (sym/anti) with the energy label (primary/secondary).
x2A_014.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. At 0 mV, Na+ would still flow in because of its gradient. Zero is not an equilibrium for Na+.
Wrong. E_K is near -90 mV, but K+ is no longer the main ion crossing. The trap is anchoring on the resting state.
Wrong. The pump keeps gradients over time, but it cannot hold the voltage when permeability changes this much.
Correct. Membrane voltage moves toward the equilibrium potential of the ion the membrane is most permeable to. For Na+ that is about +60 mV.

p: Equilibrium potential is the voltage where an ion's concentration push and electrical push cancel. E_Na is about +60 mV and E_K is about -90 mV.
The membrane voltage (Vm) is pulled toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion crosses most easily. At rest that is K+. At the peak of an action potential it is Na+.

x2A_020.eli: A tug-of-war where the strongest team pulls the flag to its side.
mem: Vm moves toward E of the most permeant ion.
E_Na about +60 mV; E_K about -90 mV.
Action potential upstroke = Na+ permeability rises.
x2A_020.trap: Picking the resting values (-70 or E_K) when the question says permeability has changed.
x2A_020.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. The amount of Na+ that enters is a tiny fraction of the cell's total Na+. The trap is imagining big concentration changes.
Correct. A membrane stores charge like a small capacitor. Moving a tiny number of ions changes the voltage a lot. The concentration barely moves.
Wrong. The gradient stays essentially intact. Thousands of spikes can fire even with the pump blocked.
Wrong. During depolarization, Na+ enters the cell, so it does not leave.

p: Voltage is about charge separated across the membrane. Only a very thin layer of ions next to the membrane needs to move to change voltage by about 100 mV.
The cell holds far more Na+ than moves in one spike. So concentration is almost unchanged. The pump slowly fixes the small drift over time.

x2A_022.eli: Adding one drop of dye to a swimming pool changes its color at the surface for a moment, but the pool's total water barely changes.
mem: One spike moves very few ions.
Concentration gradients stay almost unchanged per spike.
Na+ enters during depolarization; K+ leaves during repolarization.
x2A_022.trap: Thinking an action potential changes bulk concentrations a lot.
x2A_022.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Multipass transmembrane proteins have many hydrophobic helices inside the bilayer. They need detergent to be removed.
Correct. Peripheral proteins stick to the surface through ionic and hydrogen bonds. High salt breaks those bonds, and the protein comes off without damaging the bilayer.
Wrong. The lipid anchor sits inside the bilayer. Salt cannot pull it out, so detergent is needed.
Wrong. A single-pass protein still has a hydrophobic helix embedded in the bilayer. Salt does not remove it.

p: Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer by hydrophobic regions. Peripheral proteins sit on the surface, held by electrostatic (charge) attractions.
High salt or a pH change breaks charge attractions. Detergent is needed to dissolve the bilayer and free integral proteins.

x2A_025.eli: A sticker held on by weak tape (peripheral) comes off with a quick peel, but a nail hammered into the wall (integral) needs a tool.
mem: Salt or pH wash releases peripheral proteins.
Detergent is needed for integral and lipid-anchored proteins.
Integral proteins have hydrophobic regions in the core.
x2A_025.trap: Forgetting that lipid-anchored proteins are still stuck in the bilayer.
x2A_025.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Tight junctions seal the gap between cells so fluid cannot leak between them. They do not connect the insides.
Wrong. Desmosomes are spot welds for strength. They do not open a channel between cells.
Wrong. Hemidesmosomes anchor a cell to the basement membrane below it, not to a neighbor.
Correct. Gap junctions are channels (connexons) that link the cytoplasm of two cells. Ions and small molecules like a dye pass through. This also lets heart muscle spread electrical signals.

p: Cells connect in different ways. Some seal, some glue, and some open tunnels. Gap junctions are the tunnels. They let ions and small molecules (up to about 1 kDa) pass directly.
In the heart, this lets electrical signals pass from cell to cell so the muscle contracts together.

x2A_031.eli: Tight junctions are caulk, desmosomes are rivets, and gap junctions are little doors between neighbor houses.
mem: Tight = seal; desmosome = strong adhesion; gap = communication.
Hemidesmosome attaches cell to basement membrane.
Gap junctions are made of connexons (connexins).
x2A_031.trap: Picking tight junctions because they also 'join' cells. They seal, but they do not connect cytoplasm.
x2A_031.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Peripheral proteins are often quite mobile, so being peripheral does not predict low recovery.
Wrong. A more fluid region would make Y move faster and recover more, not less.
Wrong. Smaller proteins usually diffuse faster. That would raise recovery.
Correct. Low recovery means most of Y cannot move into the bleached spot. That happens when Y is tied to the cytoskeleton or other fixed structures.

p: FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching) bleaches a spot of fluorescent proteins with a laser. Then you watch whether unbleached proteins move in to refill it.
The final recovery percent tells you the mobile fraction. Low recovery means most proteins are stuck in place. The speed of recovery tells you how fast they diffuse.

x2A_037.eli: Erase a spot on a crowded dance floor. If dancers move in to fill it, they are free. If the spot stays empty, they are stuck in place.
mem: Final recovery percent = mobile fraction.
Recovery speed = diffusion rate.
Low recovery = tethered or immobile proteins.
x2A_037.trap: Mixing up the amount of recovery (how many can move) with the speed of recovery.
x2A_037.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. Na+ is actually smaller than K+, so a narrow pore would let Na+ through more easily. The trap is assuming selectivity is just size.
Wrong. Both Na+ and K+ have a +1 charge.

Correct. In water each ion wears a shell of water molecules. The filter's carbonyl oxygens are spaced to replace that shell for K+. Na+ is smaller and cannot touch them all, so shedding its water is too costly.
Wrong. Channels are passive. Selectivity comes from the shape and spacing of the filter, not from ATP.

p: Ions in water are surrounded by water molecules (a hydration shell). To enter a channel, an ion must give up that shell.
The K+ channel filter is lined with carbonyl oxygens spaced to stand in for water around K+. Na+ is too small to fit these oxygens well, so it stays hydrated and is kept out.

x2A_046.eli: A glove that fits one size of hand perfectly. A smaller hand slides around loosely and does not get a grip.
mem: K+ channel filter uses backbone carbonyl oxygens.
Na+ is smaller than K+ in size; both are +1.
Selectivity is a precise energy fit, not just pore size.
x2A_046.trap: Assuming a smaller ion would pass any pore a larger one can.
x2A_046.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Wrong. In normal cycling the receptor is recycled to the surface, not destroyed. The LDL goes on to the lysosome.
Correct. The endosome is acidified by H+ pumps. Low pH changes the receptor's shape so it lets go of LDL. The receptor then returns to the cell surface.
Wrong. The clathrin coat falls off soon after the vesicle forms. It does not separate LDL from its receptor.
Wrong. Endosomes are acidic, not alkaline.

p: LDL carries cholesterol. It binds the LDL receptor at the cell surface, where the pH is neutral (blood). The pocket is pulled in as a clathrin-coated vesicle.
Inside the cell, the endosome becomes acidic. Acid weakens the receptor's grip, so LDL is released and sent to a lysosome. The receptor goes back to the surface to be reused.

x2A_048.eli: Like returning a shopping cart: you drop off your groceries inside, then the cart is rolled back to the front door for the next shopper.
mem: Endosome pH is acidic.
Low pH releases cargo from receptor.
Receptors recycle; LDL goes to lysosome.
x2A_048.trap: Choosing lysosomal digestion of the receptor. Recycling is the normal route.
x2A_048.academic: Written from standard MCAT content and independently fact-checked by a second AI reviewer. Not verified against AAMC 2025-26, Wikibooks, LibreTexts or Lehninger; expert review recommended.

ox: Correct. Transferrin uptake fell when clathrin was removed, so it needs clathrin-mediated endocytosis.
Wrong. Transferrin is a large protein and cannot diffuse across the bilayer. Also its uptake fell when clathrin was removed.
Wrong. Dye uptake by macropinocytosis did not change, so macropinocytosis does not need clathrin.
Wrong. Macropinocytosis continued without clathrin. So not all endocytosis needs it.

p: A knockdown lowers the amount of one protein. If a process stops, it needs that protein. If it continues, it does not.
Clathrin forms the coat of one kind of vesicle. Macropinocytosis is a different route driven by actin that takes in large gulps of fluid.

x2A_049.eli: If one road is closed and only the cars using it get stuck, you know which cars were using that road.
mem: Process lost after knockdown = process needs that protein.
Clathrin is used in receptor-mediated endocytosis.
Macropinocytosis is actin-driven and clathrin-independent.
x2A_049.trap: Overgeneralizing from one pathway to all endocytosis.

ox: Correct. Removing most outside Na+ barely changed the voltage, so Na+ was barely contributing at rest. Resting Na+ permeability is low compared with K+.
Wrong. The question says choline is impermeant, so it cannot cross.
Wrong. If Na+ mattered most, removing it would shift the voltage a lot (more negative). It did not.
Wrong. Nothing in the question points to the pump, and a pump change would not explain a stable voltage.
